source: Owner message to the maintainer chat, 2026-10-15, paraphrased here: this repository is public and the rule itself is about not writing conversation text verbatim.
owner_request_summary: The owner observed that, at least in ChatGPT, a GitHub write tends to fail when it carries exact conversation output, while a de-identified version with the useful information extracted goes through. He asked for this to be written down as a rule so it does not have to be rediscovered.
problem: Chats file bug reports and suggestions to GitHub (suggested-fix items and uda-lane pull requests). When a chat tries to write the conversation's exact output, the write tends to fail, and each chat has had to find the de-identified form again. Exact conversation text also does not belong in a public repository.
required_behavior: An item or a uda-lane pull request filed from a chat gives the useful content in the filer's own words: what was asked, what went wrong, the evidence in summary, and the change wanted.
It quotes only the short excerpts needed to show the failure and leaves out personal details.
The owner's observation is recorded as observed, with its cause unknown.
If the extract also fails, the chat reports that to the owner. It does not retry the same content in another form or through another route.
The item format in suggested-fixes/README.md and the lesson index carry the rule; a regression test protects the text.
scope: Filing through the suggested-fix lanes and the uda-lane pull-request route from a chat. It does not change what a project may store privately in its own repository, and it is not a way around a refused write.

origin.notes: The wording of the rule is the maintainer's; the observation and the request are the owner's.

execution_surfaces.surface: patterns/suggested-fix-queue.md step 3, suggested-fixes/README.md item format and LESSON-INDEX.md entry 63

nonclaims: The cause of the failed writes is not known; this records the owner's observation and does not claim which ChatGPT check refuses them.
Text-presence tests protect the rule's wording; they do not prove that a chat writes extracts or that an extract is always admitted.
